pos: n. (a child-guardian who conducted a boy to his teacher; the Authorized Version's rendering of the law's office before Christ)
etymology: Greek paidagogos, from pais (child) and ago (to lead) — not the teacher but the household servant who walked the boy to school and kept him in order on the way. The Authorized Version renders it schoolmaster; the point is custody and conduct, not instruction.
biblical_def: “Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24). Paul is arguing that the law never was a means of justification and never pretended to be. Before faith came, Israel was “kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed” (Galatians 3:23) — held in custody, hemmed in, unable to escape the verdict of its own commandments. The schoolmaster does not teach the boy his lessons; he delivers him to the one who will. So the law delivers the sinner to Christ, and it does so by condemning him, closing every other door, and leaving him with nothing to plead. That is the law working exactly as God appointed it to work. And the office terminates: “But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster” (Galatians 3:25). The believer is not lawless — the moral law remains the rule of his obedience — but he is no longer in the custody of a covenant that could only accuse him. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth” (Romans 10:4). The schoolmaster brought him to the door and handed him over.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a schoolmaster as the man who presides over a school and instructs, and notes the scriptural sense of a conductor and guardian.
webster_full: SCHOOLMASTER, n. The man who presides over and teaches a school; a teacher, instructor or preceptor of a school.
2. He or that which disciplines, instructs and leads.
PEDAGOGUE, n. A teacher of children; one whose occupation is to instruct young children; a schoolmaster.
2. Among the Greeks, a servant who attended the sons of the wealthy, and conducted them to school.
CUSTODY, n. A keeping; a guarding; care, watch, inspection, for keeping, preservation or security.
scriptures: Galatians 3:24
Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
Galatians 3:25
But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.
Galatians 3:23
But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed.
Romans 10:4
For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.
corruption_summary: The verse is read as though the law were a kindly tutor improving us by degrees, when Paul's figure is custody and arrest.
corruption_paragraphs: The common misreading turns the schoolmaster into an educator and the law into a curriculum of moral self-improvement: the law teaches us to be good, and Christ finishes the course. Paul says the opposite. The paidagogos was not the instructor; he was the slave who kept the boy from wandering and marched him where he was told to go. The law does not make a man better and hand a partly-finished saint to Christ. It shuts him up (Galatians 3:23), stops his mouth, and delivers him as a condemned man to the only Saviour there is. Every scheme that treats the commandments as a ladder — medieval merit, Tridentine infused righteousness, modern moralistic preaching that makes the sermon a list of steps — has mistaken the guard for the teacher.

The other error runs the opposite way and abolishes the law altogether, reading Galatians 3:25 as though the Christian were released from God's commandments as a rule of life. Antinomianism has never been able to explain why the same apostle who wrote this chapter also wrote that the law is holy, just, and good, and told the Ephesians to honour father and mother. The 1689 Confession draws the line where Scripture draws it: believers are freed from the law as a covenant of works, not from the law as the rule of obedience. The schoolmaster's custody is over; the Father's house has not become lawless.
roots_summary: Greek paidagogos (G3807), a child-conductor — Galatians 3:24-25, 1 Corinthians 4:15; the Authorized Version renders it schoolmaster and instructor.
roots_lines: Greek paidagogos (G3807) — the servant who led a boy to school; Galatians 3:24, Galatians 3:25, 1 Corinthians 4:15.
Greek sugkleio (G4788) — to shut up together, to hem in; Galatians 3:22, Galatians 3:23, the custody the schoolmaster enforced.
Greek telos (G5056) — end, goal, termination; Romans 10:4, where Christ is the law's end for righteousness.
1 Corinthians 4:15 keeps the distinction sharp: ten thousand instructors, but not many fathers — the paidagogos was never the father.
Galatians 4:2 continues the household picture with tutors and governors, the heir under age differing nothing from a servant.
usage: “The law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ” — the office is custody, and it ends at the door.
“We are no longer under a schoolmaster” — freed from the law as covenant, not from the law as rule.
The schoolmaster taught no lessons; he only made sure the boy arrived.

pos: n. pl. (first elements or rows of a thing; in Paul, the elementary principles of the world under which men are held in bondage)
etymology: Greek stoicheia, the plural of stoicheion, a thing standing in a row — the letters of an alphabet, the first steps of a discipline, the rudimentary elements of a system. The Authorized Version renders the same word rudiments in Colossians and elements in Galatians.
biblical_def: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Colossians 2:8). The rudiments are the ABCs of a religion that never gets past its own alphabet: rules about meat and drink, holy days, new moons, sabbaths, touch not, taste not, handle not. Paul calls them of the world because they belong to the order that is passing, and he sets them against Christ, in whom dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. To go back to them after Christ is not devotion but regression. “Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances” (Colossians 2:20). The Galatians made the same turn and Paul is blunter with them: “Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world” (Galatians 4:3), and to return is to go back to what is “weak and beggarly” (Galatians 4:9). Weak, because it cannot justify; beggarly, because it has nothing to give. The believer has not graduated from the rudiments by mastering them but by dying to them in Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rudiment as a first principle or element, the first slight appearance of anything not yet developed.
webster_full: RUDIMENT, n. A first principle or element; the first rules or first slight appearance of anything.
2. The original of anything not yet fully formed; as the rudiments of a plant.
ELEMENT, n. The first or constituent principle or minutest part of anything.
2. The first or lowest rule; the first ground of an art or science.
BEGGARLY, a. Mean; poor; in the condition of a beggar; extremely indigent.
scriptures: Colossians 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Colossians 2:20
Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances,
Galatians 4:3
Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world:
Galatians 4:9
But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?
corruption_summary: Paul warns against the rudiments of the world, and the warning is now aimed almost anywhere except at the religion of rules it was written against.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 2:8 has become the church's favourite verse against learning as such: philosophy is read as any careful thinking, and the text is used to excuse a ministry that will not study. Paul qualifies his own noun in the same breath — philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world. He is naming a specific counterfeit at Colosse, a mixture of Jewish ceremonial rule-keeping and speculation about angels, not condemning the mind. The Reformers, who read Aristotle and wrote confessions of extraordinary intellectual rigour, understood the difference. A church that quotes this verse to justify shallowness has fallen into a rudiment of its own.

The deeper corruption is the one Paul actually addressed and it never went out of fashion: adding a rule to Christ and calling the addition maturity. Rome added a treasury of merit and a calendar of obligation; the holiness codes of later revivalism added abstinences Scripture never commanded and made them tests of fellowship. Every such system flatters the flesh, because a rule can be kept outwardly and a heart cannot be reformed by touching nothing. Paul's verdict stands over all of them: these things “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.” The regulative principle is the safeguard — what God has commanded is required, what He has not commanded is not to be bound on the conscience.
roots_summary: Greek stoicheion (G4747), an element or first principle — Colossians 2:8, 2:20; Galatians 4:3, 4:9; Hebrews 5:12; 2 Peter 3:10.
roots_lines: Greek stoicheion (G4747) — a thing in a row, an element; rendered rudiments in Colossians 2:8 and 2:20, elements in Galatians 4:3 and 4:9.
Greek sulagogeo (G4812) — to carry off as spoil; Colossians 2:8, the only occurrence, and a stronger word than deceive.
Greek philosophia (G5385) — Colossians 2:8, its only occurrence in the New Testament, and qualified there by vain deceit.
Hebrews 5:12 uses the same root for the first principles of the oracles of God — rudiments that are proper to infancy and improper to remain in.
Galatians 4:9 names them weak and beggarly: weak because they cannot justify, beggarly because they have nothing to bestow.
usage: “After the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” — the two are set against each other.
“Weak and beggarly elements” — Paul's estimate of every rule added to the gospel.
To return to the rudiments after Christ is regression, not devotion.

pos: n. (one who makes a testament or will; in Hebrews, the one whose death gives the covenant its force)
etymology: Latin testator, from testari, to bear witness, to make a will. The Greek behind it in Hebrews 9 is diatithemai, the participle of the verb from which diatheke — covenant, testament — is formed.
biblical_def: “For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator” (Hebrews 9:16). The writer is pressing a point the whole epistle exists to make: the new covenant is in force because Christ died. The Greek word diatheke carries both senses — a covenant God cuts with men, and a testament that disposes an inheritance — and Hebrews 9 works the second sense deliberately. A will is a dead letter while the man who wrote it lives; his heirs have a promise and nothing in hand. “For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth” (Hebrews 9:17). So the inheritance named in the everlasting covenant waited on a death, and the death was the Testator's own. “And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance” (Hebrews 9:15). This is why the blood is not incidental. “Without shedding of blood is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22) is not a ritual preference but the law of the testament: the heirs inherit because the Testator died, and He lives again to execute His own will.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a testator as a man who makes and leaves a will or testament at death.
webster_full: TESTATOR, n. A man who makes and leaves a will or testament at death.
TESTAMENT, n. A solemn authentic instrument in writing, by which a person declares his will as to the disposal of his estate and effects after his death.
2. The name of each general division of the canonical books of the sacred Scriptures; as the Old Testament; the New Testament.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession.
MEDIATOR, n. One that interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them.
scriptures: Hebrews 9:16
For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator.
Hebrews 9:17
For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth.
Hebrews 9:15

And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance.
Hebrews 9:22
And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.
corruption_summary: The death of the Testator is treated as a moving example rather than the legal instrument that conveys the inheritance.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern preaching regularly reduces the cross to a demonstration — God showing how much He loves us, Christ modelling self-giving. Hebrews 9 will not permit it. A testament is a legal instrument, and the writer's whole argument turns on a point of law: the will does not operate until the testator dies. An example changes nothing about an estate. Only a death transfers it. The moral-influence theory of the atonement, revived by Abelard and made respectable again by nineteenth-century liberalism, empties this chapter of its argument, because an influence conveys no inheritance and remits no transgression.

The second error runs through the sacramental systems that must repeat the death because they cannot rest in it. The Roman mass re-presents the sacrifice at every altar; Hebrews answers that Christ was “once offered to bear the sins of many,” and that a testament executed once needs no re-execution. Here the figure is exact and decisive: no man reads his father's will a second time to make the estate transfer again. The Testator died, the will is in force, and the heirs' part is to receive what has already been conveyed to them.
roots_summary: Greek diatheke (G1242), covenant or testament — Hebrews 9:15-17; the participle diathemenos (G1303) is the testator himself.
roots_lines: Greek diatheke (G1242) — covenant, testament; 33 occurrences, and Hebrews 9 turns on its double sense.
Greek diatithemai (G1303) — to appoint, to make a will; its participle is the testator of Hebrews 9:16-17.
Greek kleronomia (G2817) — inheritance; Hebrews 9:15, the eternal inheritance the testament conveys.
Greek mesites (G3316) — mediator; Hebrews 9:15, 1 Timothy 2:5 — one Mediator, and He is the Testator too.
Hebrews 9:22 gives the law of the instrument: without shedding of blood is no remission.
usage: “There must also of necessity be the death of the testator” — the cross as legal instrument, not illustration.
“Of no strength at all while the testator liveth” — the inheritance waited on a death.
The Testator died and rose; He executes His own will.

pos: n. (a dividing wall; in Ephesians, the barrier between Jew and Gentile which Christ has broken down)
etymology: Latin partitio, a dividing, from partiri, to divide. The Greek in Ephesians 2:14 is phragmos, a fence or hedge, joined to mesotoichon, a middle wall — the barrier that stood between.
biblical_def: “For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Ephesians 2:14). In Solomon's house a partition of gold stood before the oracle (1 Kings 6:21), and in the second temple a stone barrier stood between the court of the Gentiles and the courts where Israel might come, carrying an inscription that promised death to the foreigner who passed it. Paul, who had been accused of bringing a Greek past that very wall, takes the image and says the wall is down. It came down not by tolerance but by execution: “Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace” (Ephesians 2:15). The ceremonial ordinances that marked Israel off — circumcision, the food laws, the calendar — had done their work and were nailed to His cross. What follows is not that the Gentile is tolerated at a distance but that he is naturalised: “Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). One new man, one body, one Spirit, one access unto the Father.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines partition as the act of dividing, and that which divides — a wall or septum separating apartments.
webster_full: PARTITION, n. The act of dividing, or state of being divided.
2. Division; separation; distinction.
3. That by which different parts are separated; a wall which separates apartments in a building.
ENMITY, n. The quality of being an enemy; the opposite of friendship; ill will; hatred.
RECONCILE, v.t. To conciliate anew; to call back into union and friendship the affections which have been alienated.
scriptures: Ephesians 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
Ephesians 2:15
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
Ephesians 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
1 Kings 6:21
So Solomon overlaid the house within with pure gold: and he made a partition by the chains of gold before the oracle; and he overlaid it with gold.
corruption_summary: The broken wall is enlisted for every modern cause of inclusion, when the text names one wall, one cause, and one means of removal.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 2:14 is quoted at length in service of contemporary identity politics, as though Paul had announced a general programme of dismantling every boundary a society draws. The wall he names is specific: the ceremonial partition between Jew and Gentile, which God Himself had erected and which had served its purpose until the Seed came. Christ did not abolish distinctions as such — the same epistle goes on to order husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and servants. Reading the verse as a charter against all order requires ignoring the three chapters that follow it. The gospel makes one new man out of two; it does not flatten creation.

The opposite corruption is older and uglier, and the Reformed churches have not always been clean of it: rebuilding the wall on other lines — nation, tongue, or colour — while professing the doctrine that pulled it down. Every congregation that would receive a man in heaven but not at its own table has denied Ephesians 2 in practice whatever it confesses on paper. The biblical answer is not the modern grievance framework, which sorts image-bearers into oppressor and oppressed by ancestry and can therefore never reconcile anyone; it is that all are one in Adam by sin and one in Christ by grace, and that the middle wall was taken down at the cost of His flesh.
roots_summary: Greek mesotoichon (G3320), middle wall, with phragmos (G5418), a fence — Ephesians 2:14; Hebrew debir for the oracle the golden partition guarded, 1 Kings 6:21.
roots_lines: Greek mesotoichon (G3320) — middle wall; Ephesians 2:14, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek phragmos (G5418) — a fence or hedge; Ephesians 2:14, and the hedge of the vineyard parables.
Greek echthra (G2189) — enmity; Ephesians 2:15-16, what the wall expressed and the cross slew.
Hebrew debir — the oracle, the most holy place before which Solomon set his golden partition, 1 Kings 6:21.
Ephesians 2:18 names the result: through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.
usage: “The middle wall of partition” — a real barrier, in a real temple, now down.
“No more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens” — naturalised, not merely tolerated.
The wall came down by execution, not by negotiation.

pos: v.t. (to bring to nothing, to defeat, to make void; used of God defeating men, and of men attempting to void the grace of God)
etymology: Latin frustrari, to deceive or disappoint, from frustra, in vain. The Greek in Galatians 2:21 is atheteo, to set aside, to nullify, to treat as though it had no force.
biblical_def: The word runs in two directions in Scripture, and the difference is everything. God frustrates: “That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise men backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish” (Isaiah 44:25). Men attempt it against Him and fail — the enemies of the returning exiles “hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose” (Ezra 4:5), and the house was built. “The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect” (Psalm 33:10). But there is one thing a man can genuinely set aside, and Paul names it: “I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain” (Galatians 2:21). The argument is a reductio and it is merciless. If a man could be justified by keeping the commandments, the cross was an extravagance and the death of the Son of God was pointless. To add law-keeping to grace as a ground of acceptance is therefore not a small error of proportion; it is to nullify the grace and empty the death. Paul does not say the Judaizers diminish grace. He says they set it aside altogether.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines frustrate as to defeat, to disappoint, to balk, to bring to nothing.
webster_full: FRUSTRATE, v.t. To defeat; to disappoint; to balk; to bring to nothing; as, to frustrate a plan, design or attempt.
2. To disappoint; applied to persons.
3. To make null; to nullify; to render of no effect; as, to frustrate a conveyance.
VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance.
NULLIFY, v.t. To annul; to make void; to render invalid; to deprive of legal force or efficacy.
scriptures: Galatians 2:21
I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain.
Isaiah 44:25
That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise men backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish;
Ezra 4:5
And hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.
Psalm 33:10
The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect.
corruption_summary: Galatians 2:21 is read as a caution against legalistic excess, when it is a statement that law-righteousness makes the cross pointless.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is usually softened into advice about balance — do not become too rule-bound, keep grace and works in proportion. Paul allows no proportion. His sentence is an either-or with a fatal consequence attached: if righteousness comes by the law, Christ died for nothing. Trent anathematised precisely this doctrine and taught a justification by infused grace cooperating with works; every subsequent system that makes final acceptance depend on the believer's obedience — whatever its vocabulary — falls under the same verdict. The point is not that such teaching undervalues the cross. It is that, followed out, it makes the cross unnecessary.

The mirror error is to hear frustrate the grace of God and conclude that obedience is therefore indifferent, which the next chapters of Galatians demolish. Paul who wrote this verse also wrote that they which do the works of the flesh shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Justification is by faith alone, and the faith that justifies is never alone. The Reformed distinction holds the two together where the corruptions cannot: works are excluded absolutely from the ground of acceptance and required absolutely as the fruit of it.
roots_summary: Greek atheteo (G114), to set aside or nullify — Galatians 2:21, Mark 7:9; Hebrew parar and pur, to break or bring to nought — Ezra 4:5, Psalm 33:10, Isaiah 44:25.
roots_lines: Greek atheteo (G114) — to set aside, to reject, to make void; Galatians 2:21, and Mark 7:9 of rejecting the commandment of God.
Greek dorean (G1432) — in vain, without cause; Galatians 2:21, the same word rendered freely in Romans 3:24.
Hebrew parar — to break, frustrate, make void; Ezra 4:5, and used of breaking covenant.
Hebrew pur — to bring to nothing; Psalm 33:10, of the counsel of the heathen.
Isaiah 44:25 sets the pattern: God frustrates the diviner, and no man frustrates God.
usage: “I do not frustrate the grace of God” — the alternative is that Christ died in vain.
“The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought” — men are frustrated; God is not.
To add law to grace as a ground of acceptance is to void both.

pos: n. (a stone against which the foot strikes; in Romans and 1 Peter, Christ Himself to those who will not believe)
etymology: The Authorized Version's single compound for the Greek lithos proskommatos, a stone of striking-against — distinct from skandalon, the trap-stick rendered stumblingblock. The image is a rock in the road that trips the traveller who will not look.
biblical_def: Isaiah had said that the LORD of hosts Himself would be “for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel” (Isaiah 8:14) — the same stone, sanctuary to one man and ruin to another, according to whether he takes refuge in it or trips over it. Paul applies the prophecy to Israel's rejection of the Messiah: they “stumbled at that stumblingstone; As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed” (Romans 9:32-33). The reason is given in the preceding line and it is doctrinal, not accidental: they sought righteousness “not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law.” A man carrying his own righteousness cannot get past a Saviour who justifies the ungodly. Peter sets the same stone in both its offices at once: elect and precious to them that believe, and “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed” (1 Peter 2:8). The stone does not move. Men are broken on it or built upon it, and God has appointed the outcome.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a stumbling-stone or stumbling-block as any cause of stumbling, offense, or falling.
webster_full: STUMBLING-BLOCK, STUMBLING-STONE, n. Any cause of stumbling; that which causes to stumble or err.
STUMBLE, v.i. To strike the foot against an obstacle in walking, so as to fall or be in danger of falling.
2. To err; to slide into a crime or an error.
OFFENSE, n. Any transgression of law, divine or human; a crime; sin; act of wickedness.
2. That which gives displeasure; cause of stumbling.
scriptures: Romans 9:33
As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.
Romans 9:32
Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone;
Isaiah 8:14
And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
1 Peter 2:8
And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed.
corruption_summary: The offence of the stone is treated as a failure of presentation, to be removed by better manners, when Scripture locates it in the doctrine itself.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of contemporary church method assumes that if unbelievers are offended, the church has communicated badly. Remove the awkward doctrines, soften the exclusive claims, and the obstacle disappears. Scripture says the obstacle is the Stone, and the Stone is Christ. Men stumble not at the church's clumsiness but at a righteousness that is not their own — Romans 9:32 gives the reason plainly. This does not license rudeness; Peter commands meekness and fear in the same epistle. It does mean that a gospel no one can trip over is not the gospel Isaiah, Paul, and Peter preached.

The second corruption is the modern reluctance to read the last clause of 1 Peter 2:8: whereunto also they were appointed. Commentators of an Arminian cast attach the appointment to the stumbling rather than to the persons, which the grammar resists, or pass over it in silence. The Reformed churches have taken it as it stands, with the LBCF: God appoints the end and the means, and the same Stone is laid in Sion for the salvation of the elect and the just condemnation of those who reject Him. The doctrine is not an embarrassment to be managed. It is the reason a preacher may preach to anyone at all, since the outcome does not rest on his persuasiveness.
roots_summary: Greek lithos proskommatos (G3037, G4348), stone of stumbling — Romans 9:32-33, 1 Peter 2:8; Hebrew eben negeph, Isaiah 8:14.
roots_lines: Greek proskomma (G4348) — a striking against, an occasion of falling; Romans 9:32-33, Romans 14:13, 1 Peter 2:8.
Greek petra skandalou (G4073, G4625) — rock of offence; the trap-stick word, joined to the stone in both citations of Isaiah 8:14.
Hebrew eben negeph — stone of stumbling; Isaiah 8:14, where the LORD of hosts Himself is the stone.
Isaiah 28:16 lays the other side of the same stone: a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation.
1 Peter 2:6-8 sets the two prophecies together — elect and precious to believers, stone of stumbling to the disobedient.
usage: “Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence” — God lays it deliberately.
“They sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law” — the reason men trip.
Sanctuary and stone of stumbling are the same stone.

pos: adj. (miserable, afflicted, in a condition of distress; in Romans 7 the believer's honest cry under indwelling sin)
etymology: Old English wrecca, an exile or outcast, from the root that gives wreak — one driven out and miserable. The Greek in Romans 7:24 is talaiporos, worn down by hardship, wretched through toil and affliction.
biblical_def: “O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24). The cry comes at the end of Paul's account of the war between the law of his mind and the law of sin in his members, and it is not despair — the very next verse answers it: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:25). Wretchedness here is the mark of a living man. A corpse does not groan under corruption; only one who has been given a new nature can hate the old one. Moses had used the word of his own burden when he asked the LORD to kill him rather than let him see his wretchedness (Numbers 11:15). But the most terrible use is the one where the sufferer does not know: “Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17). Laodicea was wretched and comfortable. Paul was wretched and honest. The difference between them is the whole difference between a dead church and a living saint, and the counsel to Laodicea is to buy of Christ gold tried in the fire (Revelation 3:18) — that is, to become conscious of the poverty that was there all along.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wretched as very miserable, sunk into deep affliction or distress, and also worthless or despicable.
webster_full: WRETCHED, a. Very miserable; sunk into deep affliction or distress, either from want, anxiety or grief.
2. Calamitous; afflicting.
3. Very poor or mean; worthless; paltry.
4. Despicable; hatefully vile and contemptible.
MISERABLE, a. Very unhappy from grief, pain, calamity, poverty, apprehension of evil, or other cause.
scriptures: Romans 7:24
O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?
Romans 7:25
I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin.
Revelation 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
Numbers 11:15
And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favour in thy sight; and let me not see my wretchedness.
corruption_summary: The cry of Romans 7 is medicalised into low self-esteem to be cured, when it is the groan of a regenerate man under remaining sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic preaching hears O wretched man that I am and reaches for a remedy Paul never offers: a better estimate of the self. On that reading the verse describes a problem of self-perception, and the cure is to stop speaking of oneself in such terms. Paul's question is not how shall I feel better about myself but who shall deliver me from the body of this death, and the answer is a Person, not a reappraisal. The conviction is accurate. The man really is wretched in himself, and the deliverance really is outside him. Substituting self-regard for a Deliverer leaves the sin and removes the only cure.

The opposite error treats Romans 7 as a description of an unconverted man, or of a defective sort of Christian who has not yet reached a higher plane. The perfectionist strains of later revivalism made the chapter a stage to be graduated from. But the man speaking delights in the law of God after the inward man, serves it with his mind, and thanks God through Jesus Christ — none of which an unregenerate man does. The Reformed reading, held by the Puritans and written into the confessional doctrine of remaining corruption, takes the chapter as the normal experience of a believer who sees his own heart clearly. Laodicea is the warning at the other end: wretched, and unaware of it.
roots_summary: Greek talaiporos (G5005), wretched through hardship — Romans 7:24, Revelation 3:17; Hebrew ra, evil or misery — Numbers 11:15.
roots_lines: Greek talaiporos (G5005) — wretched, worn down; only twice, Romans 7:24 and Revelation 3:17, and the two uses are opposites in self-knowledge.
Greek rhuomai (G4506) — to draw to oneself, to rescue; Romans 7:24, the deliverance Paul cries for.
Greek eleeinos (G1652) — pitiable, miserable; Revelation 3:17, joined to talaiporos in the verdict on Laodicea.
Hebrew ra — evil, distress; Numbers 11:15, Moses asking not to see his own wretchedness.
Romans 7:25 supplies the answer in the same breath as the cry: I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
usage: “O wretched man that I am!” — the groan of a living saint, not a dying one.
“Knowest not that thou art wretched” — Laodicea's wretchedness was the unfelt kind.
Conviction of wretchedness is a mercy; the comfortable kind is the danger.

pos: adv. (in a manner unbefitting; in 1 Corinthians 11, of eating the Lord's Supper without discerning the Lord's body)
etymology: From un- and worthy, rendering the Greek adverb anaxios — not in a corresponding manner, unfittingly. The word describes the manner of eating, not the worth of the eater.
biblical_def: “Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:27). Paul is writing to a congregation whose gatherings had become a disgrace: the rich ate ahead of the poor, some were drunken, and the table meant to display one body displayed division instead. To eat unworthily is to eat in that manner — without discerning the Lord's body, treating the ordinance as a common meal, or coming in unrepented sin. The remedy prescribed is not withdrawal but examination: “But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28). The verb is examine and the command is eat. Paul adds that the judgment was already visible among them — “For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep” (1 Corinthians 11:30) — and then names the way out: “For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31). Self-judgment now, or the Lord's chastening after. The adverb is the hinge of the whole passage: no man is worthy, and every believer may come, provided he comes worthily.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unworthily as in a manner not deserving, or in a manner unbecoming and unsuitable.
webster_full: UNWORTHILY, adv. Not according to desert; either above or below merit.
2. In a manner unbecoming; unsuitably.
UNWORTHY, a. Not deserving; followed by of.
2. Unbecoming; vile; base; as unworthy conduct.
EXAMINE, v.t. To inspect carefully, with a view to discover truth or the real state of a thing.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 11:27
Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.
1 Corinthians 11:28
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
1 Corinthians 11:29
For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.
1 Corinthians 11:31
For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.
corruption_summary: An adverb describing the manner of eating is read as an adjective describing the eater, and tender consciences are driven from the table Christ set for them.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest pastoral damage done with this text comes from reading unworthily as though it meant being unworthy. On that reading the believer most conscious of his sin is the one who must stay away, which reverses the passage exactly: Paul's cure for eating unworthily is to examine oneself and so eat. Nobody at Corinth was worthy. The Supper is for sinners who know it. Where the sense is confused, sensitive Christians absent themselves and the careless commune untroubled — the precise opposite of what the apostle intended.

The other error is Rome's, and it turns on not discerning the Lord's body. Transubstantiation reads the phrase as failing to recognise a physical presence under the accidents of bread and wine, and builds an entire sacramental system on it. The context is against it: the body the Corinthians failed to discern was the body Paul had been writing about all along — the congregation they were dividing by their contempt for the poor. The Reformed doctrine keeps both truths without the corruption: Christ is truly present to faith by His Spirit, and the discerning required includes discerning the brethren with whom one eats. Bare memorialism loses the first; Rome loses the second along with the gospel.
roots_summary: Greek anaxios (G371), unworthily — 1 Corinthians 11:27, 29; dokimazo (G1381), to prove or examine — 1 Corinthians 11:28; diakrino (G1252), to discern — 1 Corinthians 11:29.
roots_lines: Greek anaxios (G371) — unworthily, in an unfitting manner; an adverb of manner, and only in 1 Corinthians 11:27, 29.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; 1 Corinthians 11:28, the self-examination that precedes eating, not that replaces it.
Greek diakrino (G1252) — to discern, to distinguish; 1 Corinthians 11:29, of not discerning the Lord's body.
Greek krima (G2917) — judgment; rendered damnation in 1 Corinthians 11:29, and shown by verse 32 to be the Father's chastening of sons.
1 Corinthians 11:32 closes the door on despair: when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.
usage: “Eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily” — a manner of eating, not a class of eater.
“Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat” — the command ends in eating.
No one is worthy; every believer may come worthily.

pos: n. and v. (the destruction of a vessel; in 1 Timothy, the ruin made of faith by a discarded conscience)
etymology: From ship and wreck, rendering the Greek nauageo — from naus (ship) and agnumi (to break) — to suffer the breaking of a vessel. Paul uses it once of the sea and once of the soul.
biblical_def: Paul knew the literal thing three times over: “Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep” (2 Corinthians 11:25). He then takes the word and does something far more sobering with it. Charging Timothy to war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18), he adds the terms: “Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck” (1 Timothy 1:19). The order in that sentence is the whole doctrine. What was put away was the good conscience; what was wrecked was the faith. Men do not usually reason their way out of Christianity and then begin to sin; they sin, refuse to repent, silence the conscience that accuses them, and afterwards find reasons why the faith was never true. The conscience is the ballast, and a ship that throws its ballast overboard will founder in the first heavy sea. Paul names two who did it — “Of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:20) — and even that severity has a remedial end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shipwreck as the destruction of a ship by rocks, shoals or tempest, and figuratively the destruction or ruin of anything.
webster_full: SHIPWRECK, n. The destruction of a ship or vessel by being cast ashore or broken to pieces by beating against rocks and the like.
2. The parts of a shattered ship.
3. Destruction; ruin; as the shipwreck of a fortune.
SHIPWRECK, v.t. To destroy by running ashore or on rocks or sand-banks.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 1:19
Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck:
1 Timothy 1:20
Of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.
1 Timothy 1:18
This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare;
2 Corinthians 11:25
Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep;
corruption_summary: Apostasy is explained as an intellectual conclusion honestly reached, when Paul traces it to a conscience deliberately put away.
corruption_paragraphs: The public account of leaving the faith is almost always a story about evidence — the sufferer read, thought, and could no longer believe. Paul supplies a different order of causation and he supplies it as an apostle: the good conscience is put away first, and the wreck of faith follows. The verb is active and deliberate; it is what a man does, not what happens to him. This is not a claim that every doubt is disguised sin, and the honest struggles of believers should never be handled as though it were. It is a claim that the road out generally runs through an unrepented sin the conscience was ordered to stop mentioning.

The second corruption is a misuse of this verse against the doctrine of perseverance, as though shipwrecked faith proved that the elect may finally fall. Scripture holds both truths without strain: those whom God effectually calls He keeps, and a man may hold a profession, serve in a church, and be finally lost. The Confession states it exactly — perseverance is the fruit of regeneration, and its absence reveals what was never present. Hymenaeus and Alexander are a warning to the professing, not a threat to the regenerate, and the warnings themselves are among the means God uses to keep His own.
roots_summary: Greek nauageo (G3489), to suffer shipwreck — 1 Timothy 1:19, 2 Corinthians 11:25; apotheomai (G683), to thrust away — 1 Timothy 1:19.
roots_lines: Greek nauageo (G3489) — to be shipwrecked; only twice, once literally at 2 Corinthians 11:25 and once of the faith at 1 Timothy 1:19.
Greek apotheomai (G683) — to thrust away, to put from oneself; 1 Timothy 1:19, and the deliberate act that precedes the wreck.
Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience; a favourite word of the Pastorals, held together with faith in 1 Timothy 1:5, 1:19, 3:9.
Greek strateuomai (G4754) — to war, to serve as a soldier; 1 Timothy 1:18, the warfare whose terms verse 19 supplies.
1 Timothy 1:20 shows even excommunication aimed at recovery: that they may learn not to blaspheme.
usage: “Concerning faith have made shipwreck” — the vessel is the profession, and it can break up.
“Holding faith, and a good conscience” — the second is the ballast of the first.
The conscience goes overboard before the faith goes down.

pos: n. (a roll or scroll of writing; in Psalm 40 and Hebrews 10, the book in which the Son's obedience was written before He came)
etymology: Latin volumen, a roll, from volvere, to roll — a book was a scroll before it was a codex. The Hebrew in Psalm 40:7 is megillah, a roll; the Greek in Hebrews 10:7 is kephalis, properly the knob or head of the roller round which the scroll was wound.
biblical_def: “Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me” (Psalm 40:7). The Psalm is David's, and Hebrews takes it as Christ's own words spoken on entering the world: “Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). The setting matters. The writer has just quoted the line that God did not desire sacrifice and offering but prepared a body (Hebrews 10:5), and he draws the conclusion in the next verse: “He taketh away the first, that he may establish the second” (Hebrews 10:9). The whole apparatus of bulls and goats is removed to make room for an obedience. What the volume contained was not merely predictions to be checked off but a will to be done — and the Son came saying that the roll was written about Him and that He had come to perform it. David's own line completes the sense: “I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8). Here is the active obedience of Christ in a single figure. The book was written before He came; He came to do what was written; and by that will believers are sanctified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines volume as a roll, as the ancients wrote on strips rolled on a stick, hence a book of a certain size.
webster_full: VOLUME, n. A roll; a book; primarily, a roll or turn, as the ancients wrote on long strips of bark or parchment, which they rolled on a stick.
2. A book, or a collection of sheets of paper bound together.
3. Dimensions; compass; space occupied, as of a body.
SCROLL, n. A roll of paper or parchment; or a writing formed into a roll.
MEGILLAH, Heb. a roll or volume.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:7
Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.
Psalm 40:7
Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me,
Psalm 40:8
I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.
Hebrews 10:9
Then said he, Lo, I come to do thy will, O God. He taketh away the first, that he may establish the second.
corruption_summary: The volume is treated as a book of predictions to be verified, when Hebrews reads it as a will to be performed by the Son.
corruption_paragraphs: Prophecy is often handled as though its whole function were evidential — a list of forecasts whose fulfilment proves the case. Hebrews 10 does something else with the volume. What is written in the roll is the Father's will, and the Son's answer is not this predicts me but I come to do it. Reduce Scripture to a prediction-checklist and the doctrine that this passage exists to teach — that Christ's obedience, not merely His death, is the substance of our acceptance — drops out entirely. The volume is about a will performed, and the performing is the gospel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the active obedience of Christ. It has been quietly surrendered wherever the atonement is preached as though only the last six hours mattered, and it was denied outright by those in the seventeenth century who allowed Christ's suffering to be imputed but not His law-keeping. The Reformed confessions hold the whole: the righteousness imputed to the believer is the righteousness of a life lived under the law as well as a death died under its curse. Lo, I come to do thy will — and He did the whole of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew megillah, a roll — Psalm 40:7, Jeremiah 36; Greek kephalis (G2777), the head of a scroll-roller — Hebrews 10:7, its only occurrence.
roots_lines: Hebrew megillah — a roll or volume; Psalm 40:7, and the roll Jehoiakim cut with a penknife in Jeremiah 36.
Greek kephalis (G2777) — the knob at the head of a scroll-roller, hence the roll itself; Hebrews 10:7, its only occurrence.
Greek biblion (G975) — book, scroll; joined to kephalis in Hebrews 10:7 as the volume of the book.
Greek thelema (G2307) — will; Hebrews 10:7, 9, 10 — the will written, the will done, and the will by which we are sanctified.
Hebrews 10:10 draws the conclusion: by the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
usage: “In the volume of the book it is written of me” — the Son on entering the world.
“Lo, I come to do thy will, O God” — prophecy as commission, not merely forecast.
The roll was written first; the obedience answered it.
